PCI.BIO: Dr. Liyu Zhang is a professor in the Department of Computer Science (CS) at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). Dr. Zhang have been serving as a faculty member in the CS department of UTRGV since it was founded in 2015 by Texas legislation. Before that Dr Zhang was an associate professor in CS at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB), one of the legacy institutions UTRGV was built upon. Dr. Zhang joined UTB in September 2007, shortly after he received his Ph. D. in CS from the State University of New York at Buffalo. Before that he received his M. S. (2000) and B. S. (1997) from Fudan University, Shanghai , China, both in CS.
PCI.TEACHING_INTERESTS: All courses in computer science and related courses in mathematics.
PCI.RESEARCH_INTERESTS: Dr. Zhang's research interests are theoretical computer science and its applications, with emphasis on computational complexity, complexity-based cryptography, and design and analysis of algorithms.  Dr. Zhang’s research has been sponsored by National Science Foundation and U.S. Department of Education.
PCI.SERVICE_INTERESTS: Serving as department/college/university committee members; Serving as reviewers of journal and conference proceedings as well as panelist of profession review panels.

CONGRANT.TITLE: A Prototype Study of Distance Service Systems
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Distance service systems enabling remote delivery of traditional face-to-face services such as medical or psychological counseling, instructing, and dating have been an important societal aspect more than ever in this post-pandemic period. Many efforts have been attempted to optimize several critical sub-systems to build and run such distance service systems, including communication, data storage, and data analysis based on and for artificial intelligence (AI). However, little research seems to have been done to investigate how and whether those sub-systems can be integrated while maintaining their peak performances.

In this project, we propose to implement a prototype distance service platform and use it to synthesize and evaluate existing techniques that optimize sub-systems to find out whether those techniques are still valid in an integrated environment. Based on our findings, we will then submit our recommendations regarding optimal tradeoffs among and limitations of those used techniques.

Our project will initially focus on a prototype for a remote medical diagnostic system. The selection of medical diagnostic systems is simply that it is among the distance systems with the most stringent requirements on quality and most essential for society in case of another pandemic period. Our prototype will bridge several sub-systems: audio/video communication sub-system, an electronic medical record sub-system, and an AI data analysis sub-system. Upon successful implementation, we will scale it to a more general distance service platform. The delivery of our project will consist of a working and reusable prototype of the distance system and a report containing the information as outlined above. In addition, all our implementation will be open source and benefit society.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Open Educational Resources for Telecommunications and Networking
CONGRANT.SPONORG: Texas Higher Education Coordinator Board (Sub-award through UT San Antonio)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Cybersecurity is one of the most rapidly evolving multidisciplinary fields today. A 2022 study conducted by (ISC)2 reports that the cybersecurity global workforce gap has grown to 3.4 million. More participants (43% to 48%) in the past year indicated that their organization lack proper time for assessment and oversight of processes, and that they experience slow patching of critical systems and inadequate time and resources for training as a consequence of staffing shortages.

A key takeaway from the (ISC)2 report is that from 2021 to 2022, practical skills and experience have become viewed as essential qualifications for those considering employment in the cybersecurity profession (in contrast to acquiring certifications alone). One challenge in providing these skills is that technology, both hardware and software, is constantly and rapidly evolving, and workforce training must stay abreast of the opportunities and ramifications surrounding these innovations. Although cybersecurity programs are proliferating in secondary and higher education, many do not have the resources to design, update, and deploy relevant and technical hands-on content in a collaborative environment. Our goal is to educate the next generation of cybersecurity students with the creative problem-solving skills and investigative mindset they need for today’s workforce. To address these industry challenges we propose an OER Implementation Program, entitled “THECB Cybersecurity Foundations: Telecommunications and Networking”.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Privacy-Preserving Medical LLMs: Federated Learning with Robust Aggregation Guided by Large-Scale Evaluation
CONGRANT.SPONORG: Texas Academy of Medicine, Engineering, Science and Technology
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The project aims to develop a federated learning (FL) framework tailored for distributed medical data that preserves privacy while supporting multi-modal integration. It will design efficient aggregation strategies to manage noisy, heterogeneous, and potentially adversarial client updates, and incorporate a large-scale supernet model as a meta-evaluator, leveraging knowledge distillation to improve model performance, fairness, and explanation quality. Ultimately, the project seeks to deliver a scalable and transferable framework that can serve as a model for secure and trustworthy medical AI deployment across diverse healthcare systems.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Enhancing the Security of IoBT Infrastructure with Decentralized Ledger

PI: Hansheng Lei
Co-PI: Xu Lei, Liyu Zhang, Fitra Khan, Mahmoud Quweider

Motivation and challenges. The Internet of Things (IoT) aims at to build an architecture to integrate a wide variety of devices for computation, sensing, communication, and actuation. This concept is then extended to the Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) that can connect all types of units in the battlefield to enable predictive analytics for intelligent command and control and battlefield services. Considering the complexity of IoBT deployment environment, an edge-cloud architecture is a suitable way to connect IoBT devices. Edge computing datacenters are deployed closer to the physical places where IoBT devices are used, and this allows data to be collected and processed locally. IoBT applications running in different edge computing datacenters only need to interact with each other through the cloud datacenter when necessary. Therefore, this architecture greatly reduces unnecessary communication and latency. Furthermore, the edge-cloud paradigm is also consistent with the design of 5G network, which is believed to be critical for DoD. Systems built on top of an IoBT infrastructure, especially systems involving AI, rely on data collected by IoBT for making support decisions and conducting operations of critical infrastructure. A failure of preserving the integrity of such a system can cause serious consequences. However, there is a lack of end-to-end protection of IoBT and systems built on top of it, especially AI systems, which prevents fully unleashing the potential of IoBT.
The goal. The goal of the proposed efforts is to provide end-to-end protection of key IoBT applications, which is achieved through the following objectives: (i) A novel blockchain architecture that is designed to work with IoBT and able to handle a large number of IoT devices in an efficient manner; (ii) an end-to-end IoBT infrastructure protection mechanism based on the newly proposed blockchain architecture, especially for AI systems built on top of it; and (iii) a prototype implementation of the proposed framework and a testbed environment for benchmarking.
Technical approach. The proposed blockchain based end-to-end IoBT protection solution consists of two major components: (i) A novel blockchain scheme that is integrated with edge-cloud architecture and able to support a large number of IoBT devices; and (ii) an integration of the protection mechanism into the proposed blockchain scheme to guarantee the effectiveness of IoBT applications running in the edge-cloud environment. The novel blockchain scheme consists of multiple edge-blockchains and one cloud-blockchain, where multiple edge-blockchains can support massive number of IoBT devices, and the new protocols proposed herein allow each of the blockchains to verify information stored on other blockchains in an efficient way. This novel blockchain scheme is then leveraged to protect AI systems through two steps: protecting the data collection procedure and protecting the model building procedure, which is usually expensive and hard to verify. Due to the immutability feature of blockchain and our novel stochastic checking mechanism, an adversary cannot compromise the integrity of an AI system without tampering with the majority of the peers of the proposed blockchain system.
Expected results. The expected results of the proposed efforts are three-fold: (i) The design and implementation of the edge-cloud blockchain and integrated protection mechanism for IoBT applications, especially AI related applications; (ii) a testbed to benchmark the developed system and future systems such as distributed asynchronous processing and analysis of things; and (iii) involving undergraduate and graduate students in research and development in IoT and IoBT areas.

Edge computing datacenters are deployed closer to the physical places where IoBT devices are used, and this allows data to be collected and processed locally. IoBT applications running in different edge computing datacenters only need to interact with each other through the cloud datacenter when necessary. Therefore, this architecture greatly reduces unnecessary communication and latency. Furthermore, the edge-cloud paradigm is also consistent with the design of 5G network, which is believed to be critical for DoD. Systems built on top of an IoBT infrastructure, especially systems involving AI, rely on data collected by IoBT for making support decisions and conducting operations of critical infrastructure.  A failure of preserving the integrity of such a system can cause serious consequences. However, there is a lack of end-to-end protection of IoBT and systems built on top of it, especially AI systems, which prevents fully unleashing the potential of IoBT. 
The goal. The goal of the proposed solicitation is to provide end-to-end protection of key IoBT applications, which is achieved through the following objectives: (i) A novel blockchain architecture that is designed to work with IoBT and able to handle a large number of IoT devices in an efficient manner;  (ii) an end-to-end IoBT infrastructure protection mechanism based on the newly proposed blockchain architecture, especially AI systems built on top of it; and (iii) a prototype implementation of the proposed framework and a testbed environment for benchmarking.
Technical approach. The proposed blockchain based end-to-end IoBT protection solution consists of two major components: (i) A novel blockchain scheme that is integrated with edge-cloud architecture and able to support a large number of IoBT devices; and (ii) an integration of the protection mechanism into the proposed blockchain scheme to guarantee the effectiveness of IoBT applications running in the edge-cloud environment. The novel blockchain scheme consists of multiple edge-blockchains and one cloud-blockchain, where multiple edge-blockchains can support massive number of IoBT devices, and the new protocols proposed herein allow each of the block-chains to verify information stored on other blockchains in an efficient way. This novel blockchain scheme is then leveraged to protect AI systems through two steps: protecting the data collection procedure and protecting the training procedure. Due to the immutability feature of blockchain, an adversary cannot compromise the integrity of an AI system without tampering with the majority of the peers of the proposed blockchain system.
Expected results. The expected results of the proposed solicitation are three-fold: (i) The design and implementation of the edge-cloud blockchain and integrated protection mechanism for IoBT applications, especially AI related applications; (ii) a testbed to benchmark the developed system and benchmark future systems such as distributed asynchronous processing and analysis of things; and (iii) involving undergraduate and graduate students in research and development in IoT and IoBT areas.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant Introductory Sequence to Build Computational Skills
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Computational knowledge and skills have become essential to all disciplines and economic sectors. The ubiquity of computing impacts how we educate and prepare the future workforce regardless of one’s chosen career pathway. Thus, it is imperative to develop non-CS undergraduate students’ essential skills in solving problems computationally in their discipline and in possessing knowledge of ethical concerns related to growing cyber threats and vulnerabilities. To address this need, three institutions of higher education are collaborating as a Networked Improvement Community [NIC]: The University of Texas at El Paso [UTEP], Texas A&M University Corpus Christi, and the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. The aim of improvement at each institution is to raise non-CS students’ motivation to pursue knowledge of computational skills and become aware of ethical and security issues. The proposed project has three objectives to meet its goal of developing non-CS students’ skills for solving problems using computation: (1) develop and refine outcome-focused, problem-based, discipline-relevant course modules for creating course sequences that are adaptable to varying institutional context and disciplinary degree programs; and (2) incorporate inclusive practices into delivery of the modules to retain and advance students in the computational sequence.

Intellectual Merit. UTEP is the lead institution and Alliance Backbone of the NSF-funded National CAHSI (Computing Alliance for Hispanic-Serving Institutions) INCLUDES Alliance. The Alliance aims to broaden participation of Hispanics in computing using the conditions of collective impact, an improvement science framework closely aligned with NICs. With its 12-year history of building and supporting academic partnerships, CAHSI and its Backbone team are well positioned to support the IHE partnership in the proposed work, which aligns with CAHSI’s mission of growing and sustaining a networked community focused on advancement of Hispanics in computing. The proposed project has defined a collection of modules focused on problem-solving, computational thinking, cybersecurity, and ethics that can be used to create a sequence for STEM, non-CS majors that is adaptable to local context. In addition, the Alliance Backbone will support the professional development of instructors involved in the project with evidence- and research-based inclusive practices, which are especially important for success of Hispanics and other individuals from underrepresented groups. Using the improvement science framework with feedback from the external evaluator, the investigators and STEM subject matter experts from the partner institutions will critically review and iteratively improve organizational structures, course modules, and sequences. The investigators have expertise in working with interdisciplinary projects and are committed to collaborate in refinement of a reconfigurable, introductory course sequence designed to prepare the future STEM workforce with computational knowledge and skills.

Broader Impacts. The partner institutions are Hispanic-Serving Institutions [HSIs] with majority Hispanic populations. Working with non-CS departments, the project will serve a significant number of women who are over-represented in the partnerships’ STEM fields (other than Physics) involved in the project. This has potential to broaden participation of students from underrepresented groups in computing, a priority of the NSF. The proposed modules are adaptable across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. Because the Alliance operates as a network of networks, it has numerous outlets for disseminating modules to both Alliance institutions and other HSIs. One such outlet is the Alliance’s non-profit-organization partners, Excelencia in Education and Great Minds in STEM, that are national Hispanic organizations sharing a core purpose of increasing the number of Hispanics who are competitive in higher education generally and in computing specifically.

CONGRANT.TITLE: TRUSTVILLE: Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Getting students’ interest piqued in a college degree in a STEM field is challenging. However, due to ever increasing pace of technology transformation, the area of computer science is frequently afforded an opportunity to attract students to relatively new areas with visible impact on everyday life and business. Cyber security, a field pervasively touching almost every aspect of modern life, boasts a promise of job growth of 28% from 2016 through 2026 according to BLS. On the other hand, according to ISACA, 84% of organizations believe that only half or fewer of the applicants for security jobs are qualified. This proposal is for enhancing Teaching and Research Utilizing Security Track based on a Versatile Integrated Lab for Learning Enrichment (TRUSTVILLE). The proposed integrated security lab, which includes Internet of Things (IOT) equipment as well, will be familiarizing students with the state of the art cyber security appliances and software in a realistic environment to give them a competitive edge in the job market for serving to fill the existing gap in cyber security in public and private sectors.

The Computer Science Department at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley has been offering courses in cyber security area, however, a formal cyber security track with the required training has not been offered due to lack of hardware and software. The institution has Data, Intelligence and Security (DIS) group, with its own lab space, and prides itself for hosting the first International Conference on Data, Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) in April 2018. Given the current faculty expertise in cyber security, experience in teaching related courses, having a DIS group with its own lab space and the market potential for cyber security jobs, the university is strategically poised for offering a specialized track in cyber security to enhance teaching and research.

Due to the market demand, the hardware and software related with cyber security are expensive, and this proposal is for securing funds to assist the institution’s ongoing efforts to establish a market driven cyber security track supported by a modern cyber security integrated laboratory. Since low traffic volume is encountered in a lab environment, expensive high-performance ASIC based hardware is not needed. However, the updates to the firmware and software of security hardware, and to the software itself could be as frequent as daily, for example, to block vulnerabilities including zero-day worms. Therefore, most of the expense of cyber security integrated lab is not in the hardware, but rather in the annual subscription of the software to keep the lab current.

The cyber security track in computer science will consist of seven computer science courses geared towards cyber security, three criminal justice courses, and a senior cornerstone project in the area of cyber security. All of these courses will incorporate Project Based Learning (PBL) methodology to familiarize the students with industry grade cyber security tools and appliances. The required integrated laboratory will consist of a gamut of cyber security related hardware and software to understand and analyze the weaknesses of systems and procedures and learn how to strengthen security at different levels. The integrated security laboratory will consist of software and hardware such as IoT devices, IPS, IDS, threat hunting, vulnerability management, traffic monitoring, penetration testing, forensics, encryption, network security and endpoint security for both on premise and cloud assets.

CONGRANT.TITLE: IBSS-L: The Effect of Co-Designed Accessible STREAMS Apps on Inclusion of Hispanic Pre-school Students with Disabilities
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The purpose of this interdisciplinary research study is two-fold. First, it is to investigate if pre-school general and special educators’ collaborative experience in designing and implementing cloud-based STREAMS (science, technology, reading, engineering, arts, mathematics and self-regulation)
curricular applications (Apps) for their students with disabilities influences their attitudes toward inclusion, their collaborative behaviors, and their attitudes toward their own teaching effectiveness. Second, it is to explore the effect of accessible technology-based STREAMS Apps on learning outcomes of pre-school students with disabilities (SWDs) and the engagement of their parents. Engaging students in learning of STEM at an early age is critical for preparing
these students for success in STEM careers as adults. This study addresses disparities due to ethnicity, socioeconomic status (SES), and disabilities. It is intended to garner the collaborative creative efforts and expertise of a multidisciplinary (social-behavioral-economic sciences
and education) research team housed within the Special Education Research Consortium of College of Education, P-16 Integration, University of Texas Rio Grande Valley. This study will facilitate Brownsville Independent School District in meeting their district improvement goals on pre-school
inclusion. Based on needs survey findings, STREAMS research team proposes to use two-week teacher summer institutes and three to five parent support workshops for teachers and parents to design accessible pre-school curriculum for students with disabilities (SWDs) based on Universal Design for Learning theoretical framework. Knowing the value of engaging parents of SWDs, the research team will provide parent support workshop that are family-centered and
child-focused. This 3 year project covers 16 iPads for SWDs, stipends for teacher training, incentives for parent participation, and one month pay for each team member and part-time staff assistance. Research Design: The STREAMS research team will use a mixed methodological approach to address the following research questions. 

1.What are the effects of co-designing STREAMS on teachers’ attitudes toward the collaborative experience, inclusion, and changes in teachers’ self-efficacy?
2.What are the effects of STREAMS on SWDs’ learning outcomes?
3.What are the effects of STREAMS on parental engagement in their child’s education?

The team will collect survey and interview data. In addition, the team will measure the pre-/post and one-year post differences on SWDs’ learning outcomes. This will be accomplished using
curriculum-based measures and norm-referenced instruments that measure across domains of academic and social-emotional skills. 

Intellectual Merit :
This study will contribute to STEM knowledge base in two ways. The produced curricular applications (apps) will increase pre-school children’s interest toward STEM fields and accelerate the social and cognitive learning of pre-school children with or without disabilities. Further,
very limited research studies have been done using UDL framework and principles and, of the few, the application of this framework is in math, science, and engineering (Rose & Gravel, 2010). The team of general and special teachers will operationalize UDL framework to ensure that the end product is accessible to all learners, especially SWDs, in pre-school settings.

Broader Impacts :
This study can interrupt the cycle of academic failure and develop a new trajectory for Hispanic children with disabilities. Successful SWDs’ learning outcomes reduce social costs in welfare support and empower SWDs to lead productive and fulfilled adult life through accessible technology and inclusion. It will allow opportunities for teachers to collaboratively develop evidence-based pedagogical content knowledge in STEM and will capitalize on the cultural and linguistic capitals
of young Hispanic SWDs through parental collaboration. This research project examines factors that maximize the potential of the child with disabilities for inclusion through collaborative
teaming and technology use. It will provide schools with an evidence-based inclusion model for sustainable inclusion practice and strengthen collaborative partnership between local school district and UTRGV Special Education Research Consortiums. Most importantly, it will strengthen the moral and social foundations of U.S. education and advances U.S. in building STEM education in a socially just fashion.

CONGRANT.TITLE: CUE Ethics: Collaborative Research: An Adaptable Discipline-Relevant
CSI-MAB (Computer Science Instruction using Mobile Apps with BYOD)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Mobile computing, especially in the form of smart phones and tablets, is fast replacing the
use of desktop computers and laptops. Faculty must take full advantage of this paradigm shift
by introducing the new technologies into the curriculum and the classroom. This will provide
students with a broader access and a deeper immersion into technology. Recent surveys have
shown that most of the devices students have today are connected to the internet and can run
apps capable of supporting graphics and multimedia. Faculty can judiciously integrate such
devices into their instructional approach to deliver course content to students in an individualized
manner; implement interactive and asynchronous activities; embed and collect assessment- and
instruction-related data; and facilitate communication among students. The goal of this proposal
is to create a BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) instructional model, including development of
Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) course-specific apps; implement the model in key CIS
courses; and study the impacts of model implementation on students. Key measures will include
(anticipated) improvements in student accessibility, interest and engagement, retention, and
course performance; and the model will undergo continuous evaluation and refinement. We aim
to study the effects of introducing one-to-one results-driven learning and instruction, via
personalized technology (BYOD and mobile apps), into the core CIS courses of Programming Fundamentals
I and II (PF-I, PF-II), and Discrete Structures (DS), to determine whether the new model improves
interactivity and engagement, as well as accessibility and time spent on course material.
We will assess the behavior and learning of first- and second-year students to determine specific
behavioral patterns, rates of learning concepts, and the extent to which embedded computer
science concepts are learned. The new apps will be carefully designed to cater to the typical
student at The University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB): a Hispanic, first-generation college
student with a deprived socioeconomic background. While the developed apps will have the necessary
embedded preparation and assessment modules, we will also ensure that they are rich with content:
video/audio clips, 2-D and 3-D presentations, and outside links; and that the BYOD device
should become the student’s companion and personal tutor outside the classroom. Faculty in
UTB’s CIS department will collaborate to develop multimedia-based, interactive course content
modules designed for teaching key courses of the CIS curriculum. The developed content will
be deployed through apps designed initially for the Android operating system. Faculty from
the Education department will provide embedded formative and summative assessment measures
that will be used and types of data to be collected through the interactive and data-driven
apps. Multivariate statistics will determine the effects of the variables of the apps and
assess any differences in participant behavior or learning patterns.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Promoting Postbaccalaureate Opportunities for Hispanic Americans (PPOHA) Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC) is a public four-year
university that serves more than 17,000 students, over 90 percent of whom are Hispanic coming from the
Rio Grande Valley (RGV) region in south Texas. While Rio Grande Valley is a region of tremendous
potential for growth in terms of human capital (the first in the nation) and in terms of contributions this
population can make to the state and the nation, such potential cannot be realized without the intellectual
and educational resources that have been historically lacking. The region is still plagued with a dismaying
poverty rate of 36.5 percent in 2008. There is an extremely urgent need in Rio Grande Valley to provide
affordable postsecondary education, and produce high-quality graduates with promising employability, in
order to bring radical changes to the local economy.
To respond to such severe regional situations as well as the national imperative to promote postsecondary
education for Hispanic Americans, The University of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College
proposes a project to improve its graduate programs in computer science (CS) and math as an effort to
expand postbaccalaureate educational opportunities for Hispanic Americans and contribute to the
bootstrapping of regional economy. The project aims to (1) improve the retention and graduation rates of
Hispanic and low-income graduate students in computer science and math; (2) improve the employability
including the ability for Ph.D. study of Hispanic and low-income students upon their graduations; (3)
attract more Hispanic and disadvantaged students to enter into Science, Technology, Engineering, and
Mathematics fields.
Over the life of the grant, the project will integrate proven best practices including: (1) course
development consisting of online course development to facilitate convenient access to these courses and
improve students’ retention rate, and new course development and course redesign in emerging areas such
as bioinformatics, cyber security and distance education in mathematics that will greatly benefit students’
future employment and/or further academic careers; (2) faculty mentored research to engage students in
research and keep them motivated and focused on their graduate study to prompt success; (3) high-school
outreach and teaching activities to build linkages among computer science or math students towards
teaching in high schools and motivate them to pursue a teaching career, as well as to attract more high
school teachers/students to pursue computer science and math undergraduate/graduate degrees; (4)
summer internship program to enable students to get first-hand industry experience through internships
and to be more employable upon graduation; (5) invited speaker series where successful minority
students, scholars and industry leaders will be invited as role models to the University of Texas at
Brownsville and Texas Southmost College to have dialogues with our participating students to inspire
them to pursue advanced study in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics; (6) teaming
graduate students with undergraduate students in research project as well as in regular academic life
through “buddy-mentoring” in order to not only develop the leaderships of graduate students but also
engage undergraduate students to strengthen and widen the pipeline in computer science and math
through graduate degrees.
Upon successful execution of the project, we anticipate the project outcomes to be significant increases in
enrollment, retention and graduate rates, as well as immediate employment rates in the computer science
and math graduate programs. We also anticipate an increased portion of our graduates to go on to pursue
Ph.D. degrees

CONGRANT.TITLE: Disjoint NP-pairs and Structural Properties of Complete Sets
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
A (disjoint) NP-pair is a pair of disjoint, nonempty sets in the complexity class NP. The study of disjoint NP-pairs is motivated by their relations to public-key cryptosystems and to propositional proof systems. In particular, answers to questions about existence of NP-hard or P-inseparable NP-pairs informs us about the question of whether secure public-key cryptosystems exist; existence of complete NP-pairs is implied by existence of optimal propositional proof systems. This project will investigate P-inseparable and complete NP-pairs further, in particular whether they can be derived from a hypothesis that is weaker than any of the known ones, and whether existence of these NP-pairs have strong consequences that are unknown before.  We will examine commonly (dis)believed hypotheses in complexity theory such as that NP≠coNP and that PH collapses, and research on their relations to the existence of P-inseparable and complete NP-pairs. It is also our goal to build on recent results regarding relations between NP-pairs and propositional proof systems and obtain deeper insight into both subjects.

It is important to study structural properties of complete sets because they gives us a better understanding of the computational power of various complexity classes, and also might lead to proofs of separation results in complexity theory. The proposed project will focus on the following structural properties of complete sets: 
-	Robustness: does a complete set remain complete if certain amount of elements are taken away from the set? 
-	Autoreducibility: does a complete set reduce to itself via a reduction that does not query on the input string? 
-	Mitoticity: can a complete set be split into two complete sets? 
Most complete sets have been known to have one or more of these properties. The proposed project aims to address the remaining open questions regarding these properties especially those having major impact in complexity theory if settled.  For example, are EXP-complete sets autoreducible for the truth-table reductions? Solving this problem would either separate EXP from PH, or PSPACE from P.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: BPC-DP: SUMMIT: A Joint UTB-UTA Program for Enhancing Minority Participation in Computer Science
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB) and the University of Texas at Arlington (UTA) propose a BPC demonstration project, named SUMMIT (SUstained Mentoring, Monitoring and InTeraction), to design and execute a focused but comprehensive program for improving and broadening the participation of women and underrepresented groups, such as the Hispanic community, in pursuing advanced degrees
in computer science (CS). For recruiting, nurturing, mentoring and retention of students from these communities, we propose a pilot project that is built on the principle of mentorship formed through a dual-level research experience programs that will continue throughout the whole duration of the students’
graduate study. This continued mentoring, monitoring and retention effort will result in a holistic approach that we call sustained mentoring. The goal of such mentoring is to provide continuing rather than one-time
support as well as the much needed encouragement and meaningful research experience to underrepresented but talented students. SUMMIT will establish pipelines, starting from junior years and culminating in the successful admission of the students into Ph.D. programs and subsequent graduation.

The SUMMIT pilot project is aimed at scaling into an alliance throughout the state of Texas and extending to the Gulf Coast states where such efforts are acutely needed. SUMMIT will utilize the best practices and will enhance, disseminate, and institutionalize these best practices in the region and at the national level.

The SUMMIT program encompasses the following seven major components: (1) An early recruiting and retention plan that places emphasis on early engagement, constant monitoring and encouragement; (2) A two-stage research experience program that includes an advanced research experience workshop at UTA preceded by a preparatory research experience workshop at UTB; (3) Co-advising for students by faculty members at UTA. Participating students will conduct research under co-advising and
mentoring by faculty from their home institutions and UTA. This will equip students with necessary research experience to facilitate their transition and admission to the Ph.D. program at a research
institution; (4) Student buddy-mentoring. We will match participating students with Ph.D. students at UTA who will serve as buddy-mentors to provide students with informal academic guidance as well as emotional support; (5) Invited Speaker Series. Successful minority students, researchers and scholars in computing will be invited as role models to UTB and UTA during the two respective research workshops to have dialogues with our participating students. They will be the best people to inspire students
participating in our project to pursue advanced study and research in computing; (6) A Ph.D. application workshop that includes sessions to help students prepare materials for Ph.D. admission as well as sessions to help students do well in the GRE subject test; (7) Interactive assessment and evaluation. Independent evaluators from social science will be recruited to evaluate the effectiveness of the project.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Improving Undergraduate Mathematics Learning through the Innovative Integration of Learning Theories and Touch-Screen Technologies
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The overarching goal of the project is to improve students’ success and the quality of learning
collegiate mathematics through introduction of new methodology based upon learning theories accepted by the math education community, and touch-screen technologies (iPad in particular). Touch-screen technologies will be used to create “objects to teach/learn/work with” while learning linear algebra content common for the College Algebra and Linear Algebra courses.

Significance of the Project: Incorporation of touch-screen technologies to the college curricula to address recommendations of learning theories is a new approach that, to the best of the proposers’ knowledge, has not been widely utilized so far in teaching college mathematics.

Intellectual Merit: The developed methodology and strategy will be an integration of proven learning theories findings (radical constructivism and Stage by Stage Development of Mental Action Theory) with modern touch-screens technology, (particularly I-Pads). The methodology of development of action in a material/materialized form, that involves exercises aimed at the studied properties of the model of action in a materialized form, will be developed.

Broader Impact: The project results will have a potential to transform the manner in which
undergraduate math education is conducted. It will be scalable to different sizes of student populations and transformable for various areas of mathematics. The developed strategy can be easily incorporated into asynchronous online and/or blended teaching and could impact a large population of students. The developed materials will be as mobile as the I-Pad and will allow students to be engaged in learning, irrespective of their location. A large predominately Hispanic student population will be positively impacted.

Project’s Objectives: (1) Improve student disposition toward mathematics; (2) Improve understanding of algebra as a process of modeling and problem solving that produces results; (3) Develop and introduce into teaching of the content that Linear Algebra and College Algebra have in common methodology/strategies that are based on integration of the onstructivism/SSDMA and touch-screen technologies. Create learning materials that support these methodologies/strategies; (4) Develop iPad applications to teach elements of Linear Algebra; (5) Develop mathematics faculty expertise in applying learning theories to teaching collegiate
mathematics; (6) Enhance the understanding of how students learn mathematics at the collegiate level in the Touch-Screen Learning Environment in general and iPad in particular: conduct an assessment on how the “quality” of “objects to work with” impact teaching undergraduate mathematics at different levels.

Assessment of students’ disposition & understanding dynamics: The team will conduct qualitative assessment to identify aspects of student disposition toward mathematics and understanding of algebra and how those dispositions and understanding change through the use of the iPad learning environment.

Evaluation: The project will be evaluated by the external evaluator, who is an expert in the field.

Dissemination: The project’s results will be disseminated through a series of workshops, publications and presentations at professional meetings and conferences, and implementation to the teaching practice of other institutions.

Collaborative project between Hispanic Serving University and Community College.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Computational Scientists with Homeland Security Skills
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This project aims to take the new Computational Science degree at the University of Texas at Brownsville and create a pathway through the degree specifically aimed at creating technical graduates with an understanding of Homeland Security issues and the ability to apply their skills to secure our border and ensure the safety of US citizens. The degree has 35 credits of technical elective subjects, some of which will be prescribed for project scholarship holders in order to ensure that they graduate with a rigorous education and a tailor-made skill set. Students will be advised on remaining electives to help them make choices appropriate to the lab, center of excellence of division of homeland security that are targeting for employment.

There are two courses that are not offered by the department of Computer Science and Computer Information Science which will be developed. These are Cyber-security and Computer Forensics. These will be developed and will become mandatory for all project scholarship holders. 

Other subjects including, Database Management Systems, Networks, Software Engineering and Image Processing will be modified to incorporate topics relevant to Homeland security (e.g., safety-critical software engineering, secure programming, data security, face recognition, secure networks) and will become required subjects.

In addition to these new and modified courses, a monthly seminar series will be introduced. This will be mandatory for project scholarship holders but available for other students to attend. The seminar series will bring in Homeland Security personnel and researchers from Centers of Excellence to discuss research issues of interest. The seminar series will help facilitate placement of students in internship and summer employment while they complete their degrees and will assist in placing students on completion of their degree. Guest speakers will also act as mentors to students.

Project scholarship holders will also be required to work for 4 hours each week over the academic year in the Homeland Security testbed that the University of Texas at Brownsville has developed. This testbed examines technology in use in border security. Students will participate in projects to improve the technology and create new applications to assist border patrol agents and immigration officers. This work will extend over the entire time the student is associated with the project and will culminate in a senior design project that has a Homeland Security focus and is developed with the involvement of a mentor from Homeland Security or n associated university Center of Excellence.

In order to raise awareness of the project and the opportunities that exist within Homeland Security, the principle investigator will produce and distribute documentation to schools within the Rio Grande Valley. In addition to school visits throughout the academic year, information nights to teachers, students and parents will also offered each semester. Homeland Security personnel will be invited to participate in these activities.

The success of the project will be tracked by maintaining contact with project scholarship holders and regularly conducting surveys and interviewing them as well as their employers. For those students that continue onto graduate school, we will track the area in which they conduct their research and where they eventually gain employment.

CONGRANT.TITLE: R&D: Using a Community of Practice Approach to Enhance the Abilities of Computer Education Teachers
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This project aims at developing an effective professional development program for high-school school teachers to address the challenge of how to enhance teachers’ abilities in computer and information sciences (CIS) education in a culturally diverse environment. The participants of our project are predominantly high-school teachers in the Brownsville Independent School District (BISD) in Texas State, who through this project will obtain degrees or credit hours needed to teach computer courses in the
Texas Dual Enrollment Program (TDEP) for high-school students. The long term goal of our project is, however, to create and foster a nourishing community of practice (CoP) among peer teachers that promotes productive learning of CIS content knowledge through interactions that develops life-long learning. For the research aspect, we will investigate whether and how such a CoP model integrated with a university-based professional development program in a minority setting will increase the CIS content knowledge and instructional skills of participants that improves their delivery of CIS content in the
classroom setting, and develop a culture that increases both instructional and CIS skills.

Our project includes the following major components: (1) a graduate program for high-school teachers leading to a master degree in education with a CIS concentration; (2) creation and maintenance of a nourishing community of practice among teachers through regular in-person formal and informal meetings, ad hoc cyber-enabled ways such as online discussion forums, and other possible means; (3)
incentive mechanisms including tuition assistance, participant stipends, and articulation agreements with high-school districts to hire only qualified teachers to teach computer courses in the future; (4) involvement of high-school teachers in the curriculum development to create a pipeline between high schools and computing degrees offered by CIS department of UTB; (5) research that investigates the
effects of the models developed in this project on CIS learning and teaching of high-school teachers in a minority setting.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: BPC-DP: SUMMIT: A Joint UTB-UTA Program for Enhancing Minority Participation in Computer Science
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB) and the University of Texas at Arlington (UTA) propose a BPC demonstration project, named SUMMIT (SUstained Mentoring, Monitoring and InTeraction), to design and execute a focused but comprehensive program for improving and broadening the participation of women and underrepresented groups, such as the Hispanic community, in pursuing advanced degrees
in computer science (CS). For recruiting, nurturing, mentoring and retention of students from these communities, we propose a pilot project that is built on the principle of mentorship formed through a dual-level
research experience programs that will continue throughout the whole duration of the students’
graduate study. This continued mentoring, monitoring and retention effort will result in a holistic approach that we call sustained mentoring. The goal of such mentoring is to provide continuing rather than one-time
support as well as the much needed encouragement and meaningful research experience to underrepresented but talented students. SUMMIT will establish pipelines, starting from freshman and culminating in the successful admission of the students into Ph.D. programs and subsequent graduation. The SUMMIT pilot project is aimed at scaling into an alliance throughout the state of Texas and extending
to the Gulf Coast states where such efforts are acutely needed. SUMMIT will utilize the best practices and will enhance, disseminate, and institutionalize these best practices in the region and at the national level.

The SUMMIT program encompasses the following seven major components: (1) A recruiting and
retention plan that places emphasis on early engagement and constant monitoring and encouragement; (2) A two-stage research experience program that includes an advanced research experience workshop at UTA preceded by a preparatory research experience workshop at UTB; (3) Co-advising for students by faculty members at UTA. Participating students will conduct research under co-advising and
mentoring by faculty from their home institutions and UTA. This will equip students with necessary
research experience to facilitate their transition and admission to the Ph.D. program at a research
institution; (4) Student buddy-mentoring. We will match participating students with Ph.D. students at UTA who will serve as buddy-mentors to provide students with informal academic guidance as well as emotional support; (5) Invited Speaker Series. Successful minority students, researchers and scholars in computing will be invited as role models to UTB and UTA during the two respective research workshops to have dialogues with our participating students. They will be the best people to inspire students
participating in our project to pursue advanced study and research in computing; (6) A Ph.D. application workshop that includes sessions to help students prepare materials for Ph.D. admission as well as sessions to help students do well in the GRE subject test; (7) Interactive assessment and evaluation. Independent evaluators from social science will be recruited to evaluate the effectiveness of the project.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Distributed Content Based Image Retrieval Systems (D-CBIR)
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
We have recently acquired a state-of-the-art data intensive and high performance computing cluster research facility, through the MRI NSF program, which we named Futuro Computing Cluster. The goal of this cluster is to foster interdisciplinary research projects and Computer Science (CS) education programs with the goal of laying a foundation for a strong research and education integration centered on CS at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB).

With the recent growth of the amount of multimedia (audio, video, and images) brought about by the proliferation of digital devices, content-based image retrieval (CBIR) systems have become an important task in computer vision and multimedia processing. Coupled with the recent advances in storage media, multiprocessors, and distributed computing, CBIR systems are ripe and well positioned to benefit greatly from distributed and parallel algorithms. The goal of this project is to devise distributed algorithms for well-proven methods in CBIR to reduce the computational complexity of the search engine to be comparable with a text or metadata based one. A second goal is to take full advantage of the available computing resource at hand. In particular, our system is aimed at creating an adaptive system that automatically decides the methodology and optimal set of parameters associated with any of the three important stages in CBIR: features extraction, similarity measures, and decision schemes. The system’s adaptivity should extend to selecting a specific algorithm based on the available computing resources. Existing feature extraction algorithms including color features (such as those based on histograms, moments), texture features (such as those based on Markov random fields, Gabor filters, and wavelets), shape features (such as those based on Fourier descriptors, digital topology) are usually presented for single thread and/or single machine; the same goes for similarity measures (such as the L1 or L2 norms, Min-Max ratio), and many clustering and classification methods (such as K-means, Support Vector Machines, Subspace methods). Our proposed distributed CBIR will be reporting results on different computer architectures including Peer to Peer, Client-Server, and Cluster based. The set of available cooperative nodes can be configured adaptively to provide specific time or space constraints. Depending on the computing resources available, we will investigate the use of both software and hardware supported threads with single and multi-core processors to take full advantage of the available resources.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Research: BPC-DP: A Joint UTB-UTA Program for Enhancing Minority Participation in Computer Science Graduate Programs
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
An effective way to enhance student participation and retention in advanced degrees in computing is to engage them in faculty-mentored research (i.e., provide encouragement and support). This is, however, often a daunting challenge for a typical Hispanics serving institution (HSI) due to its limited research
resources. To establish and strengthen the education pipeline at the level of Ph.D. programs and to broaden participation in computing among Hispanics students (BPC-HS) in a mutually beneficial way, the Department of Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB), an HSI, and the Department of Computer Science and Engineering (CSE) at the University of Texas at Arlington (UTA), an institution with well established research programs, propose a collaborative project that bridges the master’s program at UTB with the Ph.D. program at UTA. This partnership will enhance opportunities for UTB students to gain research experience by pursuing Ph.D. degrees in a cutting-edge
research environment at the Department of CSE at UTA. The program will also serve as a catalyst to improve the enrollment and retention of CIS graduate students at UTB and to create Hispanic role models in computing for the future by guiding them to pursue a lifelong career in computing.

The proposed BPC-HS program will be accomplished through the implementation of the following six major components: (1) A recruiting plan that places emphasis on intervention and prevention of dropouts, and also takes the cultural advantage of UTB in the region; (2) Course alignment: The graduate CS courses at UTB will be aligned against those at UTA so that UTB students will fulfill the course requirements for Ph.D. admission by UTA-CSE upon completion of their master’s study; (3) Faculty co-advising and student buddy-mentoring: Master’s students at UTB will conduct research under joint advising by faculty from both UTB and UTA. This will equip students with necessary research experience to facilitate their transition and admission to the Ph.D. program at UTA. Student buddymentoring
will provide students with emotional support and academic guidance; (4) Summer research
workshop: This will be hosted by UTA for UTB master’s students in order to further enhance their research experience; (5) GRE subject test preparation sessions: Faculty members in the Department of CIS at UTB will hold special sessions to help students prepare for the GRE subject test to make them competitive in meeting the Ph.D. admission requirements of the CSE department at UTA; (6) Interactive
assessment and evaluation: The faculty at both universities will participate in assessing the individual progress of the students and evaluating the overall success of the program.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of Futuro: A Data Intensive and High Performance Computing Cluster for Integrated Research and Education
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The computing research instrument acquisition described here – of the Futuro computing cluster for interdisciplinary research projects and Computer Science (CS) education programs – seeks to lay the foundation for a strong research and education integration centered on CS at the University of Texas at Brownsville (UTB), a minority serving institution in the south Texas Rio Grande Valley, a historically underrepresented region with more than 90% Hispanics. The MRI investment will enable promising young investigators to greatly raise the stature of CS research at UTB and in the region, attract new
sources of research support, and elevate CS education for Hispanic students to a competitive level.

The south Texas valley region has 9 higher education institutions, including research institutions UTB and UT Pan American (UTPA). However, the entire valley does not have a single up-to-date cluster. The current clusters at UTB and UTPA are decommissioned after years of intensive usage. Temporary “cluster” consisting of several PCs is set up to carry on our research projects, which is very limited and non-reliable. Futuro–to be acquired and operated by UTB and shared with UTPA–will serve as a laboratory in which: core research can be conducted at a world-class level; collaborations with on-campus
domain sciences provide real-world test applications and expertise to drive significant advances in interdisciplinary research; and significant opportunities are made available to both undergraduates and graduates in CS and related disciplines.

Intellectual Merit: Futuro will enable research activities in data mining, pattern discovery, genetic data analysis, experimental astronomical physics, collaborative filtering, theory of computation, high dimensional visualization, and other computational areas. More precisely, it will enable the following activities with transformative goals: (1) terabyte scale data mining and pattern discovery in time series
datasets obtained from heterogeneous sensor network; and applying this research to address important data analysis problems in Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO), one of the nation’s most advanced scientific endeavors on the frontiers of physics; (2) Genetic data analysis in complex human diseases to identify totally novel susceptibility factors; this research will enable new
understanding of genetic causes of complex diseases such as schizophrenia and thus likely lead to development of new therapeutic strategies for them; (3) studying the dynamical systems and Stellar populations to model the behavior of black hole binaries in globular clusters and galactic nuclei; this research will create models of formation of stellar systems via intensive computation and they can
provide important information for interpretation of results from currently operating gravitational wave detectors (such as LIGO and LISA detectors); (4) exploring and creating computing-effective, scalable, robust and intelligent learning algorithms for large recommender systems based on collaborative filtering by incorporating multispectral information; this research will lead to development of next generation recommender systems; (5) visualizing high-dimensional streaming data from heterogeneous sensors; this
research will lead to development of new data reduction methodologies, new visualization methodologies that incorporate intelligent computation such as data mining, and thus more advanced visualization systems that has cross-disciplinary utility; and (6) benchmarking and developing algorithms for approximating the NP-hard subgraph isomorphism problem with best possible practical performance; this research will benefit several import application areas such as image recognition and bioinformatics.

Broader Impact: The computing services enabled by Futuro will benefit potential users from physics, bioinformatics, computational engineering, and environment engineering at UTB and UTPA. Futuro forms a nucleus for collaboration between computer scientists and researchers from other departments
and other institutions, resulting in further funding opportunities. The project’s educational activities will train students in the Rio Grande Valley, in areas of computer science that are expected to have the greatest national impacts in the coming years. More precisely, the CS curriculum will be enriched by lab modules enabled by the cluster facility for providing hands-on experience in parallel programming and
scientific computing. As part of the proposed activities, students from computer science, physics and other programs will be involved in exciting and engaging interdisciplinary collaborative research.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Integrating Synchronous and Asynchronous Components into Graduate Curriculum to Improve Learning Effectiveness and Better Serve Students with Time Constraints
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Hispanics lag behind other major ethnic groups in attaining postsecondary degrees, especially
Master’s degrees. Most Hispanic students start their career as soon as they receive their Bachelor's degree. Later they realize that a higher degree, like a Master of Science (MS) in
Computer Science (CS), affords more opportunities and better salaries. By that time, it seems too late to return to school because they have already been involved in many responsibilities that discourage them from pursuing any advanced degree. To resolve this dilemma, they may choose between two options. The first option is that they can pursue an online degree from a select online university. However, this option lacks face-to-face interaction with faculty and fellow students which raises a concern regarding the effectiveness of distance learning. Another possibility is to choose a local university that offers both online and face-to-face instruction. Studies show that hybrid (combining online and face-to-face instruction) course offering appears
more effective in learning than face-to-face or fully Web-based instruction. Therefore, the
second option is obviously more feasible for most students.

To better serve the needs of prospective students who have interests in pursuing a higher degree, such as an MS in CS but are not able to attend traditional college due to other commitments, we propose a pilot project to integrate both synchronous and asynchronous components into our graduate curriculum that allows for reduced face-to-face instruction. The goal of the project is to improve the existing graduate program in CS by developing, implementing, and evaluating an innovative hybrid lecturing mode at the University of Texas at Brownsville/Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC), which serves approximately 17,000 students, of which over 90 percent are Hispanic.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Disjoint NP-pairs and Structural Properties of Complete Sets
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
We propose to continue research on disjoint NP-pairs and structural properties of complete sets.Both areas are active and have many interesting and important open problems. We believe that major results in these two areas will shed new lights in computational complexity and bring about a better understanding of fundamental open problems in the area.

A disjoint NP-pair is a pair of disjoint, nonempty sets in NP. The study of disjoint NP-pairs is motivated by its connections to secure public-key cryptosystems and to propositional proof complexity. The latter subject is concerned with the complexity of proof systems for propositional logic, which itself is related to the problem of whether NP equals coNP. In a reasonable formulation of public-key cryptosystems, the problem of cracking public-key cryptosystems is equivalent to separating certain disjoint NP-pairs. For this reason, answers to questions about the existence of NP-hard or P-inseparable disjoint NP-pairs informs us about the question of whether secure public-key cryptosystems exist or whether public-key cryptosystems can be NP-hard to crack.

Disjoint NP-pairs is also related to propositional proof systems. Razborov associated a canonical
(disjoint) NP-pair with every propositional proof system and showed that the canonical NP-pair of an optimal propositional proof system is complete for the class of all disjoint NP-pairs. Recently we much strengthened Razborov’s result by proving that every disjoint NP-pair is equivalent to the canonical NP-pair of some propositional proof system. We also showed that canonical NP-pairs contain certain information about their proof systems. These results display unexpected and interesting connections between disjoint NP-pairs and propositional proof systems. We would like to obtain more results along this line to gain better understandings of both disjoint NP-pairs and propositional proof systems.

It is important to study computational structures of complete sets, because they, by reductions of all the sets in the class to the complete sets, represent all of the structure that a class might have. For this reason, the study of structural properties of complete sets gave us a better understanding of the computational power of various complexity classes, and also might lead to proofs of separation results in complexity theory. We will focus on robustness, autoreducibility, and mitoticity in this project. Many complete sets have been known to have one or more of these properties while several questions still remain open. We will continue investigating on this.

This project will prompt research and education in theoretical computer science at a Hispanic-serving institution. The PI will develop senior and graduate courses and seminars to teach topics
related to this project. The PI’s graduate student will actively engage in the research of this project. We believe that successful completion of the project will greatly foster the interests among students for research in theoretical computer science and for computer science and engineering at large. This project will also contribute to broadening participation of Hispanics in computer science and engineering, who have been historically underrepresented in the area. All results from this project will be disseminated broadly. Our project will be part of the ongoing effort in the computer science community to understand the ultimate nature of computing. The long term goal is to seek answers for fundamental questions on computing such as what can be computed (efficiently) and how. We believe that any major breakthrough regarding these questions will eventually bring radical changes to computer science and information technology, which will in turn benefit human society in this age of information.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An Integrated Framework for High Dimensional Data Reduction, Data Mining, and Data Retrieval
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Technical advances in sensors and data/image acquisition modalities have resulted in a vast amount of raw and complex data in many (sometimes heterogeneous) formats. And despite the parallel increase in the capacity of storage devices and the corresponding decrease in their cost, there is still a tremendous need for novel algorithms to reduce, store, and retrieve the data more efficiently.  This need is most critical for applications involving national security functions of the army, the military, and the DoD. Therefore, to support the military needs for these efficient data processing and information extraction algorithms, we propose the creation of an integrated joint framework for combined high dimensional data reduction, image mining and retrieval representation which is based on statistical pattern recognition methods. Our proposed work will strive to connect the three areas in substantive ways, aiming at finding novel and common algorithms among them, and therefore, having the potential to reduce the time and space complexity of the overall systems or devices utilizing them.

To overcome the curse of dimensionality, our proposal seeks new and more compact data reduction algorithms by combining the best attributes of Subspace Projections methods, Clustering Methods, and Multi-dimensional Discriminant Analysis. When implemented efficiently, these methods have great effect at reducing the computational and storage requirements when either when storing images or when retrieving them. The same three methodologies will also be used for subsequent image mining and retrieval through clustering functionality, either directly or through some variation. As aside effect, the subspace projections and clustering methods can be efficiently used for visualization through pixel-based and feature-based fusion methods (for example, for multi sensors and imaging modalities). These methods strive to reduce redundant information while complimentary and characteristically intrinsic information from involved modalities is kept and utilized.

The proposal will involve our largely Hispanic students and will be closely integrated into the Computer and Information Sciences undergraduate and graduate curriculum through the following: 1) Establishment of Student DoD/CIS Scholarship/Fellowship program; 2) Establishment of the Data Reduction, Data Mining, and Data Retrieval Laboratory (D-RMRL); 3) Close one-on-one mentoring and advising by the PI and Senior Personnel; 4) Required team-projects in a set of identified courses, which include Digital Image Processing, Data Mining, Computer Vision, Databases, and Algorithm Analysis II; 5) Senior Projects and graduate theses for students who will receive fellowships;  and 6) Organization of monthly seminars by involved faculty and students.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Experimental Analysis of Algorithms for NP-hard Optimization Problems
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Efficient algorithms are among the core techniques in the advancement of many areas of computer science such as computer networking, database or emerging areas including bioinformatics or information retrieval. The past decade has seen rising interest in experimental analysis of algorithms among the computer science community; it emphasizes studying algorithms’ performance through experimental runs that mimic “typical” and common real situations. 

This project will follow the current research trend and focus on experimental analysis of algorithms for several NP-hard optimization problems (Satisfiability, Bin Packing and Traveling Salesman). NP-hard optimization problems are important in theoretical and applied computer science.  However, the best algorithms known for these problems are either approximation algorithms or algorithms with exponential time complexity. We will try to understand and implement these algorithms, carry out experimental analysis, and investigate what implementation techniques are needed to achieve their theoretical performance. Based on the results of our experimental analysis, we will also seek improvements of the algorithms, both at theoretical and implementation levels. Successful completion of the project will give us a deeper understanding of the best theoretical algorithms to-date for NP-hard optimization problems, their practical efficiency and ways of improving them. Another component of our project includes the implementations of the aforementioned algorithms that can be used in real applications and/or in competitions for those algorithms.

Besides technical goals, our project aims to strengthen research in theoretical computer science within the Department of CS/CIS at UTB.  This is critical for building a full-fledged computer science research and education program within a minority-serving institution.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Rio Grande Valley GAANN Fellowships for Graduate Study in Computer Science at UTB/TSC
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Information technology (IT) is one of the fastest-growing areas of job growth. However, statistics show that IT job growth is outstripping IT degree production for the current decade. In the current stage of economic crisis, if the U.S. economy is to remain globally competitive, we must invest in recruiting, supporting and producing more graduate degrees in the computing disciplines. This investment must occur across all segments of our population, but it is particularly important among those groups who have historically under participated in computing.  Hispanic students constitute one such population.  

The Univ. of Texas at Brownsville and Texas Southmost College (UTB/TSC) is serving over 17000 students, over 90% of which are Hispanic coming from the Rio Grande Valley  (RGV) region in south Texas. While RGV is a region of tremendous potential for growth in terms of human capital (the first in the nation) and in terms of contributions this population can make to the state and the nation, such potential cannot be realized without the intellectual and educational resources that have been historically lacking. The region is plagued with a poverty rate of 36.5%, and an estimated median household income of $28,623 in 2008, much lower than the state level $47,548 and national level $50,233. It is impossible for most students in this region to go for graduate level study without financial support. The proposed GAANN program from U.S. Department of Education will provide a critical financial leverage and create exciting opportunities so that prospective graduate students can pursue advanced CS degrees and realize their dream in an academic/industrial career.

Through the support of GAANN, the Computer and Information Sciences (CIS) department will award fellowships to graduate students who have excellent academic records and demonstrated financial needs.  CIS offers a master level program called Master of Interdisciplinary Studies with concentration in Computer Science (MSIS-CS).  MSIS has been in existence since 1992. Computer Science courses within MSIS have been offered since 2002. The proposal plans to award 3 fellowships in each fiscal year of the project. UTB/TSC is committed to match 25% of the amount of grant that Department of Education awards. To ensure that GAANN fellows maintain satisfactory progress toward the completion of their degrees, evaluation will be conducted every semester and fellowships will be renewed annually.  The goals of the GAANN project are: 1) to increase the enrollment of graduate students in the  MSIS-CS program; 2) to strengthen existing academic pipeline in CIS; 3) to enhance the GAANN fellows’ teaching skills and research capabilities; 4) to enable graduate students to concentrate on course study by providing them full financial support; and 5) to encourage GAANN fellows to pursue Ph.D. degrees in CS at doctorate institutions such as UT San Antonio, UT Dallas and UT Austin. Measurable outcomes are aligned with the goals and will be evaluated during the implementation process of the project to ensure its success.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Intensive Summer Program for SAP Probation Students at UTB
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Intensive Summer Program to be implemented at UTB/TSC aims to provide academically at-risk students opportunities to gain learning skills associated with college readiness/preparedness that will reduce their reliance on developmental education and increase the chances of success in first college-level courses. In particular, first-year students who have been put under probation by SAP (Satisfactory Academic Progress) will be selected to participate in the program. A team of 5 faculties from three departments (English, Match and Computer Science) and across the disciplines will teach entry-level courses (English 1301, Composition I; Math 0421, Introductory Algebra; and COSC 1310, Computer Literacy), featuring intensive tutoring help and one-on-one consultations, in conjunction with the services already provided by the university’s various learning enrichment programs.  The ISP proposed will identify the needs of participating students for basic learning skills and at the same time incorporate contextualized learning, with focus on helping students to grasp subject matter in sciences, into the classroom. Believing that college learning is an interactive process, the participating faculty will also introduce peer cooperative learning as an integral part of classroom activity, such as peer reviewing and group brainstorming. In addition, the faculty will hold conferences with students on a regular basis to diagnose patterns of errors and provide help tailored to each student’s special needs.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The Weaving of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence into the Fabric of Cybersecurity Curriculum: From Degree Plans to Capstone Projects
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT:
Abstract
As our newly designed degree in Cybersecurity enters its fourth year, students in the program are starting to take courses beyond the basic ones, including senior courses, technical electives, and capstone projects. While Cybersecurity is at the heart of our degree that addresses the national need for cybersecurity specialists, how we approach the education and pedagogy of cybersecurity in the era of Big Data and AI/ML (Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning) is a question that we are addressing in real-time as techniques and measures and countermeasures of cybersecurity attacks keep evolving and taking advantages of the rapid advancements in computing, memory, storage, networking, and virtualization technologies.

Educational modules with hands-on labs are available at different junctions to give students in the program multiple chances to incorporate the latest techniques in AI/ML into their degree. Whether it is advising and orientation sessions, faculty-led seminars, student-club workshops, technical electives, or capstone projects, custom-tailored material has been created specifically for our cybersecurity students. This paper presents our systematic efforts to pervade the curriculum with a hands-on, immersive approach to integrating AI/ML. We will present the following modules that were developed or are currently being developed.
